transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Optimize Suggestions beta demo - Northstar Support
Date: 2026-02-12
Time: 10:03 AM - 10:50 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Miguel Santos, Aditya Rao, Nora Ahmed
Northstar Support: Elena Park, Samir Desai, Priya Nair, Jordan Blake

Summary (auto-generated)
- Redwood demoed the new Console “Optimization suggestions” (beta) view focused on batching and caching recommendations.
- Discussion covered what “risk” means (performance/reliability risk, not security) and how Redwood labels Low/Medium/High.
- Northstar raised concerns about estimate accuracy vs billing, how assumptions are surfaced, and how to safely roll out changes with canaries/rollback.
- Next steps agreed: enable beta in staging, validate data readiness, and schedule a follow-up after Northstar sees their first suggestion set.

Topics
1) Current Northstar workload + pain points (cost volatility, p95 latency, “spiky” concurrency)
2) Suggestions list view (savings, latency deltas, risk badge, confidence)
3) Suggestion details drawer (why, assumptions, guardrails, how to apply)
4) Rollout safety (feature flags, canaries, fallback, audit trail, RBAC)
5) Accuracy + reconciliation with billing/cost attribution

Questions (captured)
- How does Redwood compute “$ / day” savings and what token price is assumed?
- What happens if traffic pattern changes after a suggestion is generated?
- Can we apply suggestions per-route and can we canary them by percent of traffic?
- Is “High risk” ever about output quality or just latency/reliability?


Transcript

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, I think we’re recording. Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. Today we wanted to show the Optimization suggestions beta in the Console. It’s the new view that surfaces batching and caching opportunities with estimated savings and also a risk label.

[00:17] Miguel Santos: Quick intros on Redwood side—Miguel, customer success. Aditya is PM for Optimize, and Nora is on the Console implementation side.

[00:27] Elena Park: Hey, Elena, I run platform here. We have Samir from ML, Priya from SRE, and Jordan from finance ops.

[00:36] Miguel Santos: Perfect. Before we jump into the UI, can you give us the quick version of what you’re trying to solve? Like what’s driving interest in this.

[00:45] Elena Park: Costs are… unpredictable. We’ve got two main chat routes, one is our “agent assist” internal tool and one is customer-facing. Customer-facing has a hard p95 target, internal is more flexible. We’re also seeing spiky QPS during business hours, like 10x.

[01:05] Samir Desai: And our cache hit rate is not great. We tried prompt caching, but the results weren’t consistent. Also we’re not sure if batching will blow up our tail latency.

[01:16] Priya Nair: Yeah, my concern is mostly rollback. Like, if this suggests we change something and it causes timeouts, we need a very clear “undo” story.

[01:27] Jordan Blake: And on my side, if you say “save $800 a day,” I’m going to ask where that number comes from and why it doesn’t match what we see in our spend dashboards.

[01:38] Miguel Santos: Great, that’s exactly what this beta is trying to address, with the caveat that these are estimates, not guarantees. Aditya will get into how we compute it and how conservative we’re being.

[01:50] Nora Ahmed: I’ll share my screen. Okay—this is the Redwood Console. You’ll see on the left nav there’s Optimize, and under that, “Suggestions (beta).” This is gated behind a feature flag right now.

[02:06] Nora Ahmed: The default view is a table. Each row is a suggestion scoped to a route + model + region. Columns: “Estimated savings,” “Latency impact,” “Risk,” and “Confidence.” Then there’s a “Last computed” timestamp.

[02:24] Samir Desai: When you say route, you mean like our API endpoint path?

[02:27] Nora Ahmed: Yes—whatever you’ve defined as a route in Redwood: it can be endpoint + project, basically the logical grouping where your traffic and SLOs are consistent.

[02:38] Nora Ahmed: Let me click into a sample org we use for demo. So here’s one: “Enable continuous batching: target batch size 6–10.” Estimated savings: $420/day, 18%. Latency impact: p50 +12ms, p95 +48ms. Risk: Medium.

[02:58] Elena Park: Okay, that’s the kind of thing we need. Where does the “Medium” come from?

[03:02] Aditya Rao: Jumping in. Risk is specifically performance and reliability risk—how likely it is to violate your latency SLO or create instability given the observed concurrency and request size distribution. It’s not security risk.

[03:15] Aditya Rao: For v0, risk is driven by a few inputs: current p95 headroom versus your configured SLO (or default SLO if not set), variability in queueing, and how aggressive the change is—for example a large batch target on a low-latency route is automatically higher risk.

[03:33] Priya Nair: So “Medium” means “maybe breaks p95” basically?

[03:37] Aditya Rao: It means there is meaningful tail risk. In the details drawer we explain the reasons: e.g., “Observed p95 is within 8% of SLO” or “High variance in inter-arrival times,” things like that.

[03:51] Nora Ahmed: Let me open the details drawer on the right. So the drawer has sections: “Why we recommend this,” “What we used,” “Assumptions,” and “How to enable.”

[04:03] Nora Ahmed: Under “Why,” it says: “Your route has sustained concurrency above 20 with short prompt lengths; continuous batching is likely to improve GPU utilization.” Under “Risk explanation,” it says: “Medium: p95 headroom is limited during peak hours; start with canary 10% traffic and cap max queue delay.”

[04:23] Elena Park: That last part is great. Is that just copy or can we actually set the queue delay cap?

[04:28] Nora Ahmed: You can set it in the config page. We deep link you right to it. We’re not auto-applying anything in beta.

[04:36] Priya Nair: Good. Because auto-apply would be a hard no for us.

[04:39] Miguel Santos: Yeah, that’s a stated non-goal for beta.

[04:43] Jordan Blake: I’m staring at the $420/day. What price is assumed? Is that our contract price or list price or what?

[04:51] Aditya Rao: Great question. Today, savings is computed from your observed token volume and current unit cost as seen by our cost attribution pipeline, then we model expected utilization improvements. If we don’t have a stable unit cost signal for a route, we fall back to an org-level blended rate and we show that in “Assumptions.”

[05:11] Jordan Blake: But does that match the invoice? Because our invoice has committed capacity for some stuff and usage for other stuff.

[05:18] Miguel Santos: For Dedicated versus Hosted, yes, it can diverge. In the drawer we show whether savings is “usage-equivalent” or “invoice-equivalent.” Right now beta is closer to usage-equivalent because we’re trying to show marginal savings from optimization. We can walk through how that would reconcile.

[05:38] Samir Desai: So it’s basically saying, “if nothing else changes, you’d burn fewer GPU seconds per token”?

[05:43] Aditya Rao: Exactly. And we explicitly avoid language like “we guarantee you’ll save $X.” It’s “estimated.”

[05:52] Elena Park: Do you show confidence intervals? Like, this could be $200 to $600.

[05:57] Aditya Rao: We show a confidence label and in the drawer we show the main drivers and data completeness. We’re not yet showing a numeric band in the table, but we have the inputs. In v0, “High confidence” generally means at least N days of steady telemetry and stable traffic shape.

[06:17] Priya Nair: What’s N? Like seven days?

[06:19] Aditya Rao: The default is 7 days for latency distributions and request rate stability, and at least 72 hours for cache metrics, but it varies by suggestion type. If it’s less, we either mark confidence low or we don’t produce the suggestion.

[06:37] Nora Ahmed: In this example, “Confidence: Medium” and it says “4 days of data; peak-hour distribution incomplete.”

[06:47] Samir Desai: Okay. Now caching suggestions—do you recommend prompt caching? Or KV cache? I always mix these up.

[06:54] Aditya Rao: Yeah, totally. In Redwood context, the caching suggestions are typically about prefix caching / KV reuse where applicable and also enabling cache policies for repeated prefixes. The UI will say “Enable prefix cache” and we’ll show expected cache hit uplift.

[07:11] Nora Ahmed: Here’s one: “Enable prefix caching for route /chat/customer.” Estimated savings $310/day, 9%. Latency impact p50 -8ms, p95 -15ms. Risk: Low.

[07:25] Elena Park: Wait why does caching reduce latency? Shouldn’t it maybe increase overhead?

[07:29] Aditya Rao: If there’s a good hit rate, you skip compute for the cached prefix, so it can reduce both cost and latency. But if your hit rate is low, you can add memory pressure and that’s where risk goes up.

[07:43] Priya Nair: Memory pressure means OOM on the GPU? Or eviction churn?

[07:47] Aditya Rao: Both. For v0, we model risk based on cache footprint relative to observed sequence length distributions, plus volatility. If the model is close to capacity, we’ll label it Medium or High and we’ll recommend caps and monitoring.

[08:04] Samir Desai: Do you account for quality risk? Like batching could change outputs? We’ve seen weirdness with some vendors.

[08:11] Aditya Rao: Batching itself shouldn’t change outputs for deterministic decoding; but in practice, some changes like timeouts, truncation, or different sampling defaults can. In this beta, “risk” is primarily latency and reliability, but we do include a note if a suggestion touches anything that could affect decoding behavior. For now, we’re not recommending anything like changing temperature or max tokens.

[08:36] Elena Park: Good.

[08:38] Nora Ahmed: Another thing: We show “stale as of.” Here, computed 6 hours ago. If it’s stale beyond a threshold, we show a banner that says “Estimates may be outdated due to traffic changes.”

[08:52] Jordan Blake: How often do you recompute? Hourly? Daily?

[08:55] Aditya Rao: Typically hourly for high-traffic orgs, daily for lower-traffic. We’ll tune that. There’s a compute pipeline that aggregates telemetry and produces suggestions in batch so the API stays fast.

[09:09] Priya Nair: On API fast—what’s the latency of the Suggestions endpoint? We’re sensitive to console pages that hang.

[09:15] Nora Ahmed: The UI calls a paginated endpoint. We’re targeting p95 under 250ms for list retrieval. It’s cached server-side per org/project.

[09:26] Priya Nair: Good.

[09:28] Miguel Santos: Maybe it’s helpful if you describe your current deployment. Are you using our Hosted API today or Dedicated?

[09:35] Elena Park: We’re on Hosted for most, but we have a small Dedicated pool for customer-facing because of throughput. Also we still use OpenAI for one legacy thing.

[09:47] Samir Desai: And we have a vLLM cluster internally we tried. But it’s been a pain with paging and keeping it stable.

[09:55] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[09:57] Nora Ahmed: Let me show filtering. You can filter by model, route, region, and suggestion type (batching vs caching). Sorting by biggest savings or highest risk.

[10:10] Elena Park: Can we filter by environment, like staging vs prod projects?

[10:14] Nora Ahmed: Yes, by project. If you map staging to a separate project, it’s straightforward.

[10:21] Priya Nair: What about RBAC? Who can see suggestions? We don’t want every developer seeing “here’s how to change prod.”

[10:28] Miguel Santos: Yep. We added a dedicated permission scope: optimize:suggestions:read. It respects org/project boundaries.

[10:36] Priya Nair: And audit logs when someone views or applies?

[10:41] Nora Ahmed: Viewing generates analytics events internally, but for customer audit logs, we log the config change actions, not just viewing a suggestion. When you click the deep link to the config page, the changes you make are recorded in audit logs like other settings.

[10:58] Elena Park: Okay, but we want some traceability that “this change came from a suggestion.” Is that captured?

[11:04] Nora Ahmed: Not perfectly yet. We have an “Apply” CTA in the drawer that we instrument, but the actual config save happens elsewhere. We’re discussing adding a “source=suggestion_id” tag on the config change event. It’s not in beta v0 by default.

[11:22] Priya Nair: That would be important for incident retros.

[11:25] Miguel Santos: Noted.

[11:27] Jordan Blake: Back to the estimate accuracy. If we enable batching and we don’t see savings, what do you do? Like do you have a feedback loop.

[11:35] Aditya Rao: We do. The Suggestions experience includes instrumentation: impression, expand, dismiss, and “apply click.” We’re also tracking post-change deltas (cost per 1K tokens, p95 latency) when we can attribute it. In beta, we’re explicitly collecting feedback when numbers feel off.

[11:55] Jordan Blake: Our finance team will ask: why does it say “$310/day” but our spend is monthly and includes commits.

[12:02] Aditya Rao: Totally. We should frame it as “marginal compute cost reduction” rather than invoice. We’re refining the copy. We can also present it as percent savings and as “tokens saved” equivalent.

[12:17] Elena Park: I like percent better. Dollar is good for execs but it triggers scrutiny.

[12:23] Miguel Santos: That’s consistent with other customers’ feedback.

[12:27] Samir Desai: Can you show a “why savings” breakdown? Like is it from higher GPU utilization, fewer prefill tokens, etc.

[12:34] Nora Ahmed: In the drawer, “Savings drivers” shows a short breakdown: “Expected throughput increase,” “Reduced idle time,” “Cache hit uplift.” It’s not super detailed in v0, but it’s more than a single number.

[12:49] Priya Nair: Rollout safety: do you have built-in canaries? Or are we doing that ourselves.

[12:55] Miguel Santos: Redwood supports rollouts—canary and A/B—via the Rollouts feature in Console. The Suggestions drawer links you to the relevant config and recommends a canary plan. But we’re not auto-creating a rollout for you in beta.

[13:12] Elena Park: So if we change batching parameters, we can apply it to 10% traffic and then ramp.

[13:17] Nora Ahmed: Yep, you can. You can define a policy: 10% for 30 minutes, then 50%, then 100%. And you can set rollback triggers based on latency or error rate.

[13:29] Priya Nair: Does it support automatic rollback? Like if p95 exceeds threshold.

[13:34] Nora Ahmed: For some metrics, yes. You can define guardrails. If guardrail triggers, it reverts to the previous config.

[13:42] Priya Nair: Okay, that’s table stakes for us.

[13:45] Samir Desai: One worry: batching might increase queueing and make tail latency worse, especially for customer-facing. Your example was +48ms p95. That could break us.

[13:55] Aditya Rao: That’s why we label Medium. And we’ll also suppress suggestions if your current p95 is already too close to your SLO. The model is conservative—if you’re within a small headroom band, it will either mark high risk or not suggest.

[14:13] Elena Park: What’s “small headroom band” in numbers.

[14:16] Aditya Rao: In v0, if p95 is within 5% of SLO, we do not recommend any batching increase beyond minimal; typically we’ll avoid it unless there is a strong cost signal and we can propose a tiny incremental change. If within 10%, it’s at least Medium and we advise canary.

[14:36] Priya Nair: That makes sense.

[14:39] Jordan Blake: I want to avoid a scenario where your suggestion says “save $X,” we do it, and then we get worse latency and no savings, and we wasted two weeks.

[14:49] Miguel Santos: Understood. The beta is meant to shorten that loop, not lengthen it. We’ll start in staging, confirm it doesn’t break, then canary in prod.

[15:00] Elena Park: Another question—what telemetry do you need from us? Is it just your standard request logs.

[15:06] Aditya Rao: Mostly we use our existing telemetry: request rate, concurrency, latency distributions, input/output token counts, cache hit/miss, and current config. If some of those are missing, you’ll get an “insufficient telemetry” empty state.

[15:23] Nora Ahmed: The empty state will say exactly what’s missing, like “No cache metrics observed” and will link to enable those metrics.

[15:31] Samir Desai: Are you storing prompts? We can’t have raw prompts retained.

[15:36] Miguel Santos: We don’t need raw prompts for this. The estimation uses aggregates—token counts, prefix hash hit rates, things like that. And it’s within your existing data handling settings.

[15:50] Priya Nair: We’ll still want to review what fields are logged.

[15:53] Miguel Santos: Of course.

[15:55] Elena Park: Can we talk about the risk badge copy? I saw “High risk” and I immediately think security risk.

[16:01] Nora Ahmed: Yeah, we’ve heard that. The badge tooltip explicitly says “Risk of latency/reliability regression.” The drawer repeats that. We’re also considering renaming to “Performance risk.” Not final.

[16:16] Aditya Rao: The current direction is to keep “Risk” but always pair it with copy: “Performance & reliability risk.”

[16:24] Jordan Blake: For exec reviews, “High risk” will get flagged.

[16:28] Elena Park: Same.

[16:30] Miguel Santos: Noted. We can also help you message internally: it’s a guardrail to encourage canary, not a blocker.

[16:39] Samir Desai: Do you ever show “High risk” suggestions at all? Like why show it if it’s too risky.

[16:45] Aditya Rao: We debated that. The reason is, sometimes the biggest savings are on routes that are currently misconfigured. We’d rather surface it with clear guardrails than hide it. But we can add filters to hide High risk by default.

[17:03] Nora Ahmed: There is a filter chip: Risk = Low/Medium/High. You can deselect High.

[17:08] Priya Nair: Good.

[17:10] Miguel Santos: Elena, for your two main routes, do you know your current p95 and SLO.

[17:16] Elena Park: Customer-facing: p95 target 900ms end-to-end, Redwood portion maybe 600ms. Internal: we can tolerate like 2 seconds.

[17:26] Samir Desai: Token output is usually 120-250. Input maybe 600-800 for customer-facing because of history.

[17:36] Aditya Rao: That’s helpful. With those sequence lengths, caching could help a lot if you have repeated prefixes, like a standard system prompt.

[17:44] Samir Desai: We do have a fixed system prompt plus a policy chunk.

[17:48] Aditya Rao: Great. That’s where prefix caching tends to be Low risk and meaningful savings.

[17:56] Jordan Blake: Do you have any customer examples where the estimate was wrong?

[18:00] Miguel Santos: Yes, and we’re using beta to learn. In early tests, some estimates were inflated when there was a mismatch between attributed token counts and the billing window, or when traffic changed significantly after computation. That’s why we added “stale as of” and more explicit assumptions.

[18:22] Jordan Blake: Okay, that makes me slightly nervous, but at least you’re acknowledging it.

[18:28] Priya Nair: Another safety thing: if we enable caching and it increases memory use, what monitoring do you recommend.

[18:34] Nora Ahmed: We link to the dashboard: cache hit rate, eviction rate, GPU memory, and p95 latency. The drawer includes “Monitor these metrics.”

[18:46] Priya Nair: And alerts.

[18:48] Miguel Santos: We can help set alert thresholds.

[18:51] Elena Park: What’s the workflow to get beta access.

[18:55] Miguel Santos: We enable a feature flag per org. We typically start with staging project. Also we ensure RBAC is set so only the right folks can view.

[19:06] Elena Park: We’ll want platform team only, at least initially.

[19:10] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[19:12] Nora Ahmed: One more UI detail: You can dismiss a suggestion. Dismiss requires a reason, like “Not applicable,” “Estimate seems wrong,” “Already doing this,” etc. That feedback helps improve ranking.

[19:28] Samir Desai: Does it come back after dismissal.

[19:31] Nora Ahmed: It can, if the underlying conditions change materially. Otherwise it stays dismissed for a cooling-off period.

[19:38] Elena Park: That’s fine.

[19:40] Jordan Blake: For us, if estimate seems wrong, I want a quick way to report it with numbers.

[19:45] Miguel Santos: We have a feedback intake that you can link to; and we can do it in a shared Slack channel as part of beta.

[19:54] Aditya Rao: Also, in the drawer we show the inputs used: “observed QPS,” “avg input tokens,” “cache hit rate,” so you can sanity check.

[20:06] Priya Nair: What if those inputs are wrong due to telemetry lag.

[20:10] Aditya Rao: Then confidence goes down, and we may show “insufficient telemetry.” We also have pipeline lag monitoring. In some cases, you might see no suggestions temporarily.

[20:24] Elena Park: Okay.

[20:26] Samir Desai: So what exactly do we change to ‘apply’ batching. Is it like max batch size.

[20:31] Nora Ahmed: It’s a few knobs: enable continuous batching, set target batch size range, and max queue delay. The suggestion gives recommended starting values.

[20:44] Samir Desai: And those are per route.

[20:46] Nora Ahmed: Yes.

[20:48] Priya Nair: Do you have a way to pin model versions so optimization doesn’t change model and confound results.

[20:54] Miguel Santos: Yes, model pinning is supported. Suggestions don’t change models in this beta.

[21:01] Elena Park: Good.

[21:03] Jordan Blake: If we want to validate savings, what report do we use.

[21:08] Miguel Santos: We’d use the token-level cost dashboard in Console, per route/model, and compare pre/post canary. Also we can export to your BI. For Dedicated, we’ll frame it as utilization improvement rather than invoice delta.

[21:27] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[21:29] Aditya Rao: The other thing: we’re intentionally conservative about overpromising. If you see a big number, you should assume it’s an upper bound scenario and validate with canary.

[21:41] Elena Park: That phrasing should be in the UI.

[21:44] Nora Ahmed: There is a disclaimer line under “Estimated savings”: “Estimates are not guarantees; validate with canary.”

[21:52] Priya Nair: Love that.

[21:55] Samir Desai: Is there any chance you suggest caching that breaks privacy boundaries? Like cross-tenant caches.

[22:01] Miguel Santos: No, caching is scoped within your org/project. There’s no cross-tenant reuse.

[22:07] Priya Nair: Okay.

[22:09] Elena Park: Can you talk about “guardrails.” Like, do you ever recommend something that violates your own constraints.

[22:15] Aditya Rao: We have guardrails that prevent recommendations if the route is tagged low-latency or if error rates are high, or if the estimator has insufficient confidence. Also we avoid recommending aggressive batching when output lengths are extremely variable because tail gets weird.

[22:35] Samir Desai: Tail gets weird is accurate, yeah.

[22:38] Nora Ahmed: (laughs) Noted.

[22:41] Miguel Santos: We’re at about the halfway mark. Anything else you want to see in the UI.

[22:47] Elena Park: I want to see if you can segment by peak hours. Like suggestions for business hours only.

[22:53] Aditya Rao: Not in v0. We compute using recent window; peak hour weighting is partially reflected but not explicitly configurable. We can add it to roadmap.

[23:05] Priya Nair: I’d also like a “safe defaults” button: start with minimal changes.

[23:10] Nora Ahmed: We can consider “recommended starting values” vs “max savings values.” Not in beta currently.

[23:20] Jordan Blake: And for me, I need a “how calculated” link that doesn’t read like marketing.

[23:26] Miguel Santos: Agreed. We’ll send the technical doc.

[23:30] Elena Park: So what do you need from us to start.

[23:34] Miguel Santos: Two things: confirm who should have access (RBAC) and confirm staging project exists with enough traffic to generate suggestions—or we can start in prod read-only.

[23:49] Elena Park: Staging has some traffic, but not huge.

[23:52] Aditya Rao: If staging is low traffic, you may not get suggestions. We can still enable and you’ll see the empty state. For real suggestions, prod is usually needed.

[24:05] Priya Nair: We can enable read-only in prod for platform team.

[24:10] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[24:12] Samir Desai: Can you confirm you’re not changing anything automatically.

[24:15] Miguel Santos: Confirmed.

[24:17] Nora Ahmed: Everything is manual in beta.

[24:20] Jordan Blake: And the “apply click” just takes you to config.

[24:23] Nora Ahmed: Exactly.

[24:25] Elena Park: One last concern: If we apply and it breaks, how quickly can we rollback.

[24:31] Priya Nair: Yeah, and does rollback require Redwood support.

[24:35] Nora Ahmed: You can rollback in Console immediately. If you’re using rollout policies, it can auto-rollback based on guardrails.

[24:44] Miguel Santos: You won’t need to file a ticket to rollback. But we’ll be on standby during initial canary.

[24:51] Elena Park: Okay.

[24:53] Samir Desai: What about multi-region. We’re in us-west and eu-central.

[24:58] Nora Ahmed: Suggestions are per region. You might see different risk per region due to different traffic shapes.

[25:06] Samir Desai: That’s good.

[25:09] Jordan Blake: Alright, I’m satisfied for now. I’m still skeptical about the $ numbers, but we can test.

[25:16] Aditya Rao: Healthy skepticism is good.

[25:19] Miguel Santos: Okay, let’s do recap and next steps.

[25:23] Miguel Santos: Redwood will enable Suggestions beta flag for your org, scoped to platform team RBAC. We’ll send over the estimator assumptions and the doc explaining usage-equivalent savings versus invoice. And then we’ll schedule a follow-up next week to look at your actual suggestions.

[25:39] Elena Park: Works.

[25:41] Priya Nair: Please include guidance on guardrail thresholds.

[25:44] Miguel Santos: Will do.

[25:46] Samir Desai: And if you can capture that “source=suggestion” in audit logs, that’d be huge.

[25:51] Nora Ahmed: I’ll take that back to the team.

[25:54] Jordan Blake: Thanks.

[25:56] Miguel Santos: Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript]

Notes
- Northstar objections centered on: (1) savings estimate reconciliation with billing/committed spend, (2) risk label interpretation, (3) rollout/rollback safety and auditability.
- Feature requests: hide High risk by default; peak-hour segmentation; stronger “how calculated” explanation; config change attribution to suggestion_id.
